transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2027-07-01 16:00 UTC | Duration: 48m | Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Samir Rao (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Sparkline Eng Mgr), Carlos Ruiz (CTO), Jing Wei (SRE), Asha (Prod)

Summary section (auto): Quick live demo of hosted chat generation; focused Q&A on streaming robustness, param tradeoffs (tokens vs latency), retry/backoff and idempotency; brief Console tour for traces and Optimize hints.

[00:00] Lena Park: okay hi everyone thanks for joining from Redwood, um quick roll call?
[00:08] Maya Patel: hey yes Maya here, thanks, um couple minutes on our side also.
[00:12] Carlos Ruiz: Carlos, CTO — excited to see the streaming behavior live.
[00:16] Lena Park: great, Diego and Samir are with me, we'll do a ~30 min hands-on and then Q&A.
[00:24] Diego Alvarez: quick context, Sparkline mentioned low-latency chat for clinician notes, about 200–800ms p95 target, right?
[00:34] Maya Patel: yeah that's the aspirational target, realistically 300–600ms would be acceptable, cost needs to be in the ballpark of our current token budget.
[00:44] Samir Rao: got it — we'll show streaming chunking, how to set up retries, and console traces for token breakdown.

[00:58] Diego Alvarez: launching the sandbox app now — bear with me, I'm connecting to the hosted endpoint using the SDK.
[01:08] [diego typing sounds]
[01:15] Diego Alvarez: so streaming here is SSE by default in our sample; you can also use websockets, both support incremental deltas, key point is the SDK exposes per-chunk latency and cumulative tokens.
[01:30] Maya Patel: SSE — do we get partial tokens if the request fails mid-stream? how do we resume?
[01:38] Diego Alvarez: good q — partial chunks are ephemeral, we recommend using idempotency keys for retry semantics on the client. If you need resume you can do a cached KV of the last chat context on your side and then do a short re-ask to the model. Redwood's runtime supports prefix cache (KV cache) server-side to avoid re-gen for common prefixes.
[01:58] Jing Wei: prefix cache — is that safe for PHI? we need to ensure data residency and KMS.
[02:06] Samir Rao: yeah security — our Private option or VPC attachment ensures that cache stays in your VPC; hosted can be configured with enterprise KMS and retention policies. We'll send the security sheet.

[02:22] Diego Alvarez: demo: sending a 120-token prompt with stream. [02:28] stream starts...
[02:30] Speaker 6: (inaudible)
[02:32] Diego Alvarez: you see chunks arriving ~every 50–150ms depending on model and batch.
[02:38] [streaming audio chime]
[02:40] Maya Patel: hmm I see the first chunk quicker than I expected, nice. Is that because of pre-warming?
[02:46] Diego Alvarez: part warm, part model architecture; also kernel selection — the runtime selects kernels and quantization path based on seq len.
[02:54] Carlos Ruiz: what's the tradeoff if we increase max_tokens? we worry about tail latency.
[03:00] Lena Park: longer max_tokens can increase tail latency because of generation time; for chat UIs we recommend a smaller max_new_tokens and use streaming so front-end shows progressive output while the backend finalizes. Also consider stop tokens and early stopping heuristics.

[03:18] Samir Rao: let's talk retries: Redwood supports automatic retries with exponential backoff for transient 5xxs, and you can configure max attempts. For idempotency provide a request_id header — our runtime will dedupe at the route layer.
[03:34] Jing Wei: if a retry happens after partial stream we have duplicate content risk — how do we handle dedupe on client?
[03:41] Diego Alvarez: good point — include a monotonic message sequence number client-side; on retry, server returns a status indicating whether the original completed. If original completed, dedupe on sequence id.

[03:58] Maya Patel: and what about token accounting for retries — will we be double-billed?
[04:04] Lena Park: retries that re-generate tokens will be billed, so we advise idempotency and client-side checks to avoid unnecessary retries. Also Optimize can suggest caching strategies and batching where appropriate to reduce regen.

[04:22] Diego Alvarez: now I'll show Console traces — switching to shared screen. [04:28] you can see per-request token breakdown, latency waterfall, kernel selection metadata, and a per-token cost estimate.
[04:36] Asha Thompson: can we get an alert when model regression occurs vs our baseline?
[04:40] Samir Rao: yes, Optimize supports quality monitoring — you provide evaluation prompts and thresholds; it will alert on regression and can tie to rollouts.

[04:55] [05:00] Diego Alvarez: weird transcription glitch there, sorry audio –
[05:04] Lena Park: no worries. Also routing policies — you can route by latency, cost, or region; for e.g. routing to a cheaper quantized variant if p90 latency is okay.

[05:20] Carlos Ruiz: about quantized variants — does that affect hallucination or quality?
[05:26] Samir Rao: some drop in quality can happen with aggressive quantization; Optimize will recommend model/quantization profiles per workload and run sample evals against your prompt set so you can choose the right tradeoff.

[05:44] Maya Patel: quick question on concurrency: we expect bursts during morning rounds, 200 concurrent requests for short prompts — how to balance batching vs latency?
[05:54] Diego Alvarez: continuous batching can reduce cost but can add a small batching window. You can set per-route SLO (latency target) and batching policy; runtime will dynamically batch while respecting SLOs — small bursts often benefit from micro-batching.

[06:12] Jing Wei: what about throttling and graceful degradation if capacity full?
[06:16] Lena Park: automatic fallback policies — route to a cheaper model variant, switch region, or use cached summaries. Redwood also supports soft-quotas and circuit-breaker style throttles to avoid cascading failures.

[06:32] Diego Alvarez: demo: now I'm simulating a transient 502 and showing retry flow. [06:37] you can see SDK exposes attempt metadata and backoff delays.
[06:44] Maya Patel: can we configure jitter? we want to avoid synchronized retries.
[06:48] Diego Alvarez: yes jitter is supported; default is randomized exponential backoff with jitter.

[07:00] Samir Rao: troubleshooting notes — common reasons for partial streams: client-side connection timeout, net issues, or server-side preemption during preemption window. We log these in Console traces so you can filter by error types.

[07:24] Asha Thompson: let's talk about data retention and PHI — we need 90-day retention and audit logs.
[07:30] Lena Park: hosted enterprise Tier supports configurable retention and audit logs; Private deployment gives full control. We'll attach the retention policy doc.

[07:44] [08:00] Diego Alvarez: switching to the sample code — here's a node sdk streaming snippet, note how we pass idempotency-key and request-seq.
[08:10] Diego Alvarez: // pseudo code: const stream = client.chat.stream({model, messages, idempotencyKey, max_new_tokens}); stream.on('delta', d => render(d)); stream.on('end', meta => console.log(meta));
[08:22] Maya Patel: do you have recommended defaults for temperature/top_p for clinical assistant?
[08:28] Samir Rao: for determinism lower temp (0.0-0.3) and narrower top_p (0.6-0.9); plus use system prompts and few-shot examples. We'll share a prompt cookbook.

[08:44] Carlos Ruiz: can we limit output length server-side? we don't want runaway responses.
[08:48] Diego Alvarez: yes max_new_tokens and server-side stop sequences; also Redwood can enforce response budget per tenant as a guardrail.

[09:00] Jing Wei: curious about cost projection: can Optimize give per-route cost forecasting?
[09:04] Lena Park: yep Console + Optimize shows token-level cost estimates and historical trend forecasting. You can also set alerts when spend > X% of forecast.

[09:18] [09:30] Diego Alvarez: little demo of Optimize suggestions — based on a short workload profile it suggests enabling prefix cache, reducing max_tokens for chat assistant, and using a 4-bit quantized variant for background summarization.
[09:44] Maya Patel: 4-bit quantization for summarization is fine but not for clinical diagnoses.
[09:48] Samir Rao: agreed — routing policies can send sensitive endpoints to unquantized or private models.

[10:00] Lena Park: ok we're ~30 mins in, let's open for questions and next steps.
[10:07] Carlos Ruiz: what metrics should we send back from our pilot to evaluate?
[10:11] Diego Alvarez: p50/p95 latency, tokens per request, failure rate (5xx), percent of retries, and sample qualitative evals for hallucination rate.
[10:22] Maya Patel: we'll add those to our pilot checklist.

[10:30] Asha Thompson: timeline — if pilot looks good, what's the path to dedicated capacity?
[10:36] Lena Park: usually after pilot we size Dedicated pools based on peak QPS and SLOs; commit terms vary (monthly/annual). We'll provide typical sizing templates.

[10:48] Jing Wei: legal/security — do you support SSO SAML and SCIM?
[10:52] Samir Rao: yes, SAML SSO and SCIM user provisioning supported, plus audit logs and RBAC. We'll add the integration guide.

[11:06] Maya Patel: last: can you provision a small sandbox with 2 GPUs so we can run latency benchmarks?
[11:12] Diego Alvarez: yes we'll provision an environment with dedicated pool for the benchmark for the week of 7/4.

[11:20] Lena Park: recap of action items and I'll share pricing ranges and security pack.
[11:24] Carlos Ruiz: great thanks Lena.
[11:28] [11:30] Meeting end: closing notes and drop of links in chat.

AUTO-GENERATED ACTION ITEMS: Lena to send SOC2, Diego to create sandbox, Maya to share payloads.
